questions_and_answers.question_text: What type of relationship do German genitive forms indicate?
Which genitive ending do specifiers with der‑nouns and das‑nouns take?
For die‑nouns and plural nouns, what ending do their specifiers have in the genitive?
Which statement about the genitive form of die‑nouns and plural nouns is correct?

answers.answer: They are the same as the nominative form

questions_and_answers.question_text: What ending do der‑nouns and das‑nouns often take in the genitive?
Which of these nouns takes an irregular genitive ending -n or -en?
Where does the genitive specifier and noun generally appear in relation to the noun or pronoun they modify?
Which personal pronoun has a genitive form in German?
How is a proper name typically used in the genitive in German?

answers.answer: With an -s or -es ending, before the noun

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which genitive ending is used for der‑ and das‑nouns ending in [s], [ts], [z] or [sch]?

articles.text:
In addition to the plural in this unit we have encountered some other new forms of nouns and specifiers:

a) Wilsons haben eine Wohnung im ersten Stock eines Etagenhauses in Frankfurt.
b) Die Angehörigen meiner Frau leben hier.
c) Möchten Sie sich mal eins meiner Bücher leihen?
d) Hier ist ein Roman des französischen Schriftstellers Cocteau.
e) Ist das nicht die neue Sekretärin unseres Kollegen Smith?

The underlined forms of the noun and specifier in the above sentences are called GENITIVE forms.  They indicate possessive relationships – the kind of relationships that are designated in English by the ’s (or -’) ending and by the preposition "of".  The GENITIVE is the fourth form, along with Nominative, Accusative and Dative forms, which German nouns and specifiers can have.  There are no other distinctive forms of nouns and specifiers.

Let us compare the Genitive forms in the above sentences with the corresponding Nominative forms and see what features distinguish them:

Genitive – Nominative

a) eines Etagenhauses – ein Etagenhaus
b) meiner Frau – meine Frau
c) meiner Bücher – meine Bücher
d) des Schriftstellers – der Schriftsteller
e) unseres Kollegen – der Kollege

The specifier and the noun both have the ending –es added to the Nominative form.  The specifier has the ending –er instead of –e; the noun has the same form as the Nominative.  The specifier has the ending –er instead of –e; the noun has the same form as the Nominative.  The specifier ends in –es instead of –e; –es is added to the noun.  The specifier has the ending –es added to the Nominative form; –es is added to the noun.

Note that in three cases – a), d) and e) above – the noun has a distinct Genitive form which differs from the Nominative form.  In two cases – b) and c) above – the noun has the same form.

Note that in a), d) and e) the specifier has the ending –es (or -s).  In b) and c) the specifier has the ending –er.

Let us now summarize what we have observed about Genitive forms:

a) Specifiers with der‑nouns and das‑nouns in the Genitive have the ending –es (or -s).  Both the der‑type and the ein‑type specifiers have the same endings: des, dieses, eines, unseres.

b) der‑nouns and das‑nouns in the Genitive have the ending –es or –s: Hauses, Schriftstellers.  A few der‑nouns have the ending –n or –en: Kollegen, Herrn, Diplomaten, Polizisten, Beamten, Bekannten.

c) The specifiers of die‑nouns and plural nouns have the ending –er in place of the Nominative ending –e (or –ie): der, dieser, meiner, ihrer.

d) die‑nouns and plural nouns in the Genitive have the same form as in the Nominative: Frau, Bank, Banken, Bücher, Bleistifte.

Here for reference and comparison are some typical Genitive forms (singular – plural):

- des Platzes – der Plätze
- des Omnibusses – der Omnibusse
- dieses Polizisten – dieser Polizisten
- meines Briefes – meiner Briefe
- des Jahres – der Jahre
- des Konsulats – der Konsulate
- dieses Hauses – dieser Häuser
- ihres Buches – ihrer Bücher
- der Dame – der Damen
- dieser Bank – dieser Banken
- unserer Schwester – unserer Schwestern

Note that der‑ and das‑nouns ending in the sounds [s], [ts], [z] and [sch] have the ending –es, as for example des Passes, des Platzes, des Hauses and des Tisches.  Note also that the writing system requires the sound [s] to be written –ss– when non‑final: Omnibusses, Omnibusse.

Otherwise, der‑ and das‑nouns of more than one syllable have –s, as for example des Konsulats, while monosyllabic der‑ and das‑nouns have either –s or –es, whichever the speaker prefers; you will hear both des Domes and des Doms, des Staats and des Staates.

Proper names have an –s (or –es) ending: Peters Haus, Marias Tochter, Herrn Meyers Wagen.

You will note that the Genitive form of the specifier and noun generally follow the noun or pronoun with which a possessive relationship is indicated: im ersten Stock eines Etagenhauses; die Angehörigen meiner Frau; ein Roman des französischen Schriftstellers.  Proper names in the Genitive, however, usually precede the noun designating the thing possessed: Kennen Sie Peters Frau? Ist das Herrn Beckers Wagen? Nein, das ist Marias Wagen.

There is one personal pronoun which has a Genitive form: wer? (“who”) has the Genitive form wessen? (“whose”).  Wessen Auto ist das? (Whose car is that?)  Wessen Sohn kennen Sie? (Whose son do you know?)
